papers.title: Clinical Reasoning: A 69-Year-Old Female Patient With Rapid-Onset Levodopa-Responsive Rest Tremor, Parkinsonism, and Gait Freezing.
papers.abstract: The evaluation of rapid-onset parkinsonism can be challenging, and the differential diagnosis encompasses a broad spectrum of etiology, management, and prognosis. We present a 69-year-old patient who developed rapid-onset resting tremor and parkinsonism with gait freezing. Her upper limb resting tremor began unilaterally but rapidly progressed to involve the contralateral limb and subsequently the lower limbs. This evolved within 3 months to also include generalized parkinsonism and a shuffling gait with prominent freezing and frequent falls. Her tremor was levodopa responsive; however, other symptoms were resistant to treatment. Through this case, we will demonstrate the diagnostic approach to rapid-onset parkinsonism, summarizing a comprehensive evaluation of history, examination, and investigations. Readers will consider atypical features revealed by examination and investigations, ultimately arriving at a conclusive and critical diagnosis not to be missed in the presentation of parkinsonism.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal dynamics and climate correlates of Parkinson disease mortality among older U.S. adults: national trends and forecasts to 2035.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson disease (PD) is an increasing cause of mortality among older adults, but national studies have generally examined mortality trends, forecasts, spatial variation, or environmental associations separately. We integrated these components to characterize U.S. PD mortality and its regional climate correlates. METHODS: This ecological time-series study used CDC WONDER mortality data for U.S. adults aged 65 years or older from 1999 to 2024. Joinpoint regression, exponential smoothing state-space forecasting with rolling-origin validation, state-level Moran's I, lagged count models, nonlinear spline analyses, and principal component analysis of regional climate metrics were applied. Nominal and Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P values were reported. RESULTS: From 1999 to 2024, PD deaths increased from 14,225 to 39,671, and the age-adjusted mortality rate increased from 41.42 to 71.58 per 100,000 population (average annual percent change, 1.99%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.54%-2.45%; P < 0.001). The conditional 2035 projection was 91.35 per 100,000 (95% prediction interval, 75.89-110.89). Across 7,502 rolling-origin predictions, mean absolute error was 9.24, root mean squared error was 12.12, mean bias was -6.48, and 95% interval coverage was 51.7%. State-level spatial autocorrelation was not evident in 2024 (Moran's I = 0.022; permutation P = 0.326). Primary lag 0-3 temperature estimates did not remain significant after multiplicity correction (adjusted P = 0.304), whereas Northeast lag 0-1 mean and apparent temperature estimates remained significant (rate ratios, 0.920 and 0.932 per 10 degrees F; both adjusted P = 0.010). papers.title: Astrocytic metabolic reprogramming in Parkinson's disease: mechanistic crosstalk and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), a neurodegenerative disorder, is predominantly characterized by the depletion of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta and the aberrant aggregation of α-synuclein (α-syn). Recent research has indicated that astrocytes not only function as indispensable supportive cells for the maintenance of central nervous system homeostasis but also act as crucial pathological regulators in the onset and progression of PD. In the context of PD pathology, astrocytes experience substantial metabolic reprogramming, primarily characterized by the dysregulation of glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism. These alterations may include context-dependent changes in glycolytic activity and mitochondrial respiration, disturbances in lipid transport and peroxidation defense, and impairments in the glutamate-glutamine cycle and glutathione metabolism. These alterations may compromise astrocytic metabolic support, antioxidant defense, and neurotransmitter homeostasis, thereby increasing neuronal vulnerability. This review examines changes in astrocytic glucose, lipid, and amino acid metabolism and how they intersect with α-syn proteostasis. We highlight a potential bidirectional interplay in which α-syn pathology may disrupt astrocytic metabolism, whereas astrocytic dysfunction, including impaired metabolic support and α-syn clearance, may further exacerbate neuronal pathology. Finally, we discuss therapeutic opportunities for modulating astrocytic metabolism and consider the challenges of translating preclinical findings into clinical interventions.

papers.title: Modelling prodromal Parkinson's disease: gastrointestinal pathology and early motor deficits in mice after transient rotenone exposure.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: Early gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is a hallmark feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet models capturing prodromal gut and brain pathology in PD remain limited. Motivated by the increased PD risk associated with pesticide exposure, we monitored motor behavior, brain pathology, and GI structure and function over 9 months following 5 daily doses of rotenone in mice. Transient rotenone exposure induced significant nigrostriatal pathology, ∼48% loss of dopaminergic neurons and increased α-synuclein aggregation in the substantia nigra, without significant changes in gross motor function. Notably, we identified pronounced GI dysfunction including reduced colonic transit velocity, altered motility dynamics, and delayed whole-gut transit. These functional changes were accompanied by enteric dopaminergic neurodegeneration, increased colonic α-synuclein accumulation, increased colonic crypt depth, and goblet cell hyperplasia with elevated mucin content per goblet cell. The findings are consistent with prodromal PD, suggesting the utility of this model for investigating early disease mechanisms and intervention strategies.

papers.title: A Pragmatic Approach for Brain-First and Body-First Classification in Parkinson's Disease: Insights from the Personalized Parkinson Project.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The brain-first versus body-first framework in Parkinson's disease (PD) proposes distinct origins of α-synuclein pathology, resulting in discrete progression patterns. Although this pathophysiological distinction implies different clinical trajectories, feasible criteria to classify subjects in large cohorts are currently lacking. OBJECTIVES: The goal was to develop a pragmatic approach for classifying brain-first and body-first PD clinical subtypes in a large early-PD cohort. METHODS: We, therefore, explored a pragmatic approach to separating these subtypes based on motor asymmetry, rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, and orthostatic hypotension, applied in a large cohort of persons with early PD (disease duration <5 years). RESULTS: Individuals classified as probable brain-first were more often tremor-dominant and showed a trend toward less constipation, after adjusting for disease duration, age and sex. CONCLUSIONS: This framework enables subtyping in many existing cohorts, potentially advancing our understanding of PD pathophysiology and facilitating targeted therapies. Validation against gold-standard measures is recommended to refine these criteria further.

papers.title: Protein adduction by multiple aldehydes contributes to α-synuclein aggregation and dopaminergic neuron loss in rat models of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Dopaminergic neurodegeneration in the substantia nigra causes the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD). The mechanisms underlying this neurodegeneration remain unclear. Aldehydes exhibit high reactivity that can covalently modify functional proteins and cause cell damage. This study aimed to characterize protein adduction by endogenous aldehydes and investigate its role in dopaminergic neuron loss in PD. Forty free aldehydes were identified in rat models of PD induced by 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) and rotenone using chemical isotope labeling coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry. Twenty-two aldehydes were found in the rat brain for the first time. In addition to lipid peroxidation, amine oxidation was the major source of aldehydes. Levels of 27 aldehyde-protein adducts in the substantia nigra and striatum were increased by 1- to 5-fold at 4-6 h after 6-OHDA injection. Consistently, most of these protein adducts were significantly increased in the rotenone model. Application of the trapping reagent phenelzine and the aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 activator Alda-1 reduced protein adduction by aldehydes and attenuated neuron loss induced by 6-OHDA injection. Twelve aldehydes covalently modified α-synuclein in 6-OHDA-treated rats, with the lysine residue in the GLSK peptide identified as the primary binding target. Aldehydes caused peptide crosslinking and aggregation of α-synuclein. Additive effects of covalent modification by aldehydes contributed to neuron death. Collectively, protein adduction by multiple aldehydes contributes to α-synuclein aggregation and dopaminergic neuron loss in rat models of PD. Multiple biogenic aldehydes, especially those from abnormal oxidation of amines, represent a novel class of toxic molecules that play a pathogenic role in PD.

papers.title: Plasma-derived hyperhomocysteinemia, PGAM5, and oligomeric α-synuclein as a biomarker panel for idiopathic Parkinson's disease.
papers.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to assess a novel panel of plasma biomarkers, comprising homocysteine (HCY), phosphoglycerate mutase 5 (PGAM5), and oligomeric α-synuclein, for the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) and to investigate the mechanistic interactions among these biomarkers. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, serum HCY was measured in all 150 patients with PD and 113 healthy controls (HCs), whereas plasma PGAM5 and oligomeric α-synuclein were assayed in subsets (80 PD/78 HC and 67 PD/89 HC, respectively). The diagnostic associated risk factors, and interrelationships of these biomarkers were analyzed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, multivariable logistic regression, and mediation analysis, respectively. Additionally, a diagnostic nomogram was constructed. RESULTS: Plasma levels of HCY, PGAM5, and oligomeric α-synuclein were significantly elevated in individuals with PD (all P < 0.001). The combined biomarker panel yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.89 for PD diagnosis, which increased to 0.93 when integrated with the rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) questionnaire score. HCY was an independent risk factor for PD and was associated with male sex, older age, hypertension, longer disease duration, and more severe motor/cognitive deficits (all P < 0.01). Oligomeric α-synuclein mediated 25.72% of the association between HCY and PD (P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This study validates a high-performance plasma biomarker panel for PD, identifies HCY as a risk factor for severe disease progression, and provides clinical evidence that oligomeric α-synuclein mediates the neurotoxic effect of HCY, highlighting a promising therapeutic target.

papers.title: Dysregulated splenic glucocorticoid sensitivity in aging and an a-synuclein transgenic mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Parkinson's disease (PD) and aging both disrupt hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis function and peripheral immune homeostasis. Whether aging or α-synuclein (α-syn) pathology alters glucocorticoid (GC) sensitivity of peripheral immune cells has not been investigated. METHODS: Using an ex vivo GC sensitivity assay, we assessed the responsiveness of isolated and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated splenocytes to the anti-inflammatory effects of increasing doses of corticosterone (CORT) in a wild-type (WT) aging cohort and in a PD α-syn transgenic mouse model and respective age-matched controls. RESULTS: Compared with splenocytes from 6-month-old WT mice, splenocytes from 20-month-old WT mice were less sensitive to 0.1 and 0.5 µM CORT. Isolated splenocytes from PD vs. control mice were less sensitive to 0.05, 0.1, and 0.5 µM CORT specifically at 16 months of age, but not at 6 or 20 months of age. As peripheral immune phenotyping revealed neither differences in HPA axis-related parameters nor in splenic GC receptor expression between PD and age-matched control mice, splenic GC resistance in PD mice at 16 months of age seems to be mediated by downstream GR signaling dysfunction. CONCLUSION: Together, our results support the hypothesis that α-syn pathology accelerates an aging-associated decline in the peripheral sensitivity to anti-inflammatory GCs and may thereby sustain systemic and neuroinflammatory processes in PD.

papers.title: Prospects of targeting GPR37 for neurotherapeutics.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: GPR37 has evolved from a proteostasis-linked liability in Parkinson's disease into a biologically diverse GPCR with potential relevance for oligodendrocyte maturation, neuroimmune resolution, and dopaminergic vulnerability. However, its therapeutic potential remains constrained by incomplete pharmacology and uncertainty regarding the receptor forms and cellular contexts most relevant for intervention. AREAS COVERED: This review evaluates the main features shaping GPR37 druggability, including N-terminal processing, receptor organization, constitutive activity, and the current deorphanization landscape. Relevant literature on GPR37 biology, pharmacology, and translational studies was critically assessed, with emphasis on receptor availability, processing, ligand reproducibility, paralog selectivity, and disease-relevant assay systems. We also discuss ecto-GPR37 as a potential Parkinson's disease biomarker linked to receptor processing. EXPERT OPINION: Progress in the field will depend less on assigning a single endogenous ligand than on developing a rigorous pharmacology toolkit that measures receptor availability, processing, and signaling in parallel. In the near term, biomarker-led and chemical-biology approaches appear more realistic than classical agonist/antagonist development.
